\chapter{Six to Ten, and One Sound Law}
\label{ch:fa-count-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{17}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say, hear and recognise every Persian number from one to ten, write the two of them made only of letters I have been taught, and explain why haft begins with h where septem begins with s.}

Five more numbers, the Iranian s-to-h rule that explains one of them, the analogy that explains the next, and the whole run of ten shuffled.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[shesh]{\fa{شش} — six, and the short vowel you cannot see}

\label{lesson:FA-C17-shesh}



\begin{quote}
Count one to five, then five to one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{شش}} — \emph{shesh} — \textbf{six}
\end{quote}

Two letters, and they are the same letter. The vowel between them is short, so Persian does not write it — which is the script chapter's rule doing exactly what it said it would: a Persian word can be read only once you have heard it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{شش}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{shash}, from Indo-European *\emph{swé\'{k}s}, \textquotedblleft{}six.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{six}, Latin \textbf{sex}, Greek \textbf{héx} and Sanskrit \textbf{ṣaṣ} are the same word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{shesh} — six
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{shesh} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{swé\'{k}s} $\to$ English \textbf{six}, Latin \textbf{sex}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{chahâr, panj, shesh}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%B4\%D8\%B4}{Wiktionary: \fa{شش}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[haft]{\fa{هفت} — seven, and the rule behind it}

\label{lesson:FA-C17-haft}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{shesh} and its English cousin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{هفت}} — \emph{haft} — \textbf{seven}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{هفت}} comes from Proto-Iranian *\emph{haptá}, from Indo-European *\emph{septm}, \textquotedblleft{}seven.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{septem}, English \textbf{seven} and Sanskrit \textbf{saptá} all keep the \emph{s}.

Persian does not, and that is not an accident about this word. \textbf{Iranian turned Indo-European \emph{s} into \emph{h} at the front of a word}, everywhere, and once you know that one change a great many Persian words stop looking foreign. Set the pairs side by side:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Sanskrit \textbf{saptá} — Persian \textbf{haft}
  \item Sanskrit \textbf{sindhu}, \textquotedblleft{}river\textquotedblright{} — Persian \textbf{hind} (and, through Persian, \textbf{India})
  \item Sanskrit \textbf{soma} — Avestan \textbf{haoma}
\end{itemize}

This is the single most useful sound law in the language for a reader who knows any European one, and a number is where it is easiest to see.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{haft} — seven
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{haft} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{septm} $\to$ Latin \textbf{septem}, English \textbf{seven}
  \item \emph{Apply:} \emph{s} at the front becomes \emph{h} — \textbf{saptá} $\to$ \textbf{haft}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{panj, shesh, haft}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%87\%D9\%81\%D8\%AA}{Wiktionary: \fa{هفت}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hasht]{\fa{هشت} — eight, and a rule that does not apply}

\label{lesson:FA-C17-hasht}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{haft}, and what Iranian did to every word-initial \emph{s}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{هشت}} — \emph{hasht} — \textbf{eight}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{هشت}} goes back to Indo-European *\emph{o\'{k}t\'{\={o}}w}, \textquotedblleft{}eight\textquotedblright{} — Latin \textbf{octō}, Greek \textbf{okt\'{\={o}}}, English \textbf{eight}. There is no \emph{s} anywhere in that history, so the rule you learned one lesson ago cannot be what put the \textbf{h} on the front.

What put it there was \emph{haft} standing next to it. Seven and eight are said together more often than almost any other pair of words, and the \emph{h}- of \emph{haft} spread onto its neighbour. A rule and an exception, one lesson apart, and the exception is the more human of the two.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{hasht} — eight
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{hasht} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{o\'{k}t\'{\={o}}w} $\to$ Latin \textbf{octō}, English \textbf{eight}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{shesh, haft, hasht}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%87\%D8\%B4\%D8\%AA}{Wiktionary: \fa{هشت}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[noh]{\fa{نه} — nine, and the word it is spelled exactly like}

\label{lesson:FA-C17-noh}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{hasht}, and why its \textbf{h} is there.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{نه}} — \emph{noh} — \textbf{nine}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\fa{ن}} and \textbf{\fa{ه}}. Both are yours from the script chapter, so this is the second of the twelve numbers you can write as well as say — the other was \textbf{\fa{سه}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{نه}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{noh}, from Indo-European *\emph{h1newn}, \textquotedblleft{}nine.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{novem}, English \textbf{nine} and Sanskrit \textbf{náva} are the same word.

Now look at the spelling against a word from the opening chapter. \textbf{\fa{نه}} is also \emph{na}, \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} — the same two letters, because the vowel that tells them apart is short and Persian does not write short vowels. Only the sentence separates \textbf{nine} from \textbf{no}.

This is the clearest case in the book of the trade the script chapter named. Persian writes fewer signs than it says, and the reader pays for it exactly here.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{noh} — nine
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{noh} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{h1newn} $\to$ Latin \textbf{novem}, English \textbf{nine}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\fa{نه}} — nun, then he
  \item \emph{Contrast:} the same two letters said \textbf{na} are \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%86\%D9\%87}{Wiktionary: \fa{نه}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dah]{\fa{ده} — ten, and the building block for nine more numbers}

\label{lesson:FA-C17-dah}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{noh} and \textbf{haft}, and what \textbf{\fa{نه}} can also mean.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{ده}} — \emph{dah} — \textbf{ten}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{ده}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{dah}, from Indo-European *\emph{dekm}, \textquotedblleft{}ten.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{decem} (and through it \textbf{decimal}, \textbf{December}), English \textbf{ten} and Sanskrit \textbf{dáśa} are the same word.

Hold on to this one. Persian builds every number from eleven to nineteen by putting a unit in front of \textbf{dah} — \emph{yâz}-\textbf{dah}, \emph{si}-\textbf{dah}, \emph{chahâr}-\textbf{dah} — so the next chapter costs one rule rather than nine words. Ten has to be learned before the teens can be, and now it is.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{dah} — ten
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{dah} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{dekm} $\to$ Latin \textbf{decem}, English \textbf{ten}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{haft, hasht, noh, dah}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AF\%D9\%87}{Wiktionary: \fa{ده}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — one to ten}

\label{lesson:FA-C17-practice}



\begin{quote}
Count one to five, then say what Iranian did to word-initial \emph{s}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Hear all ten named singly and out of order, and say each.
  \item Count backwards from \textbf{dah} to \textbf{yek}.
  \item Read the ten printed shuffled and say each.
  \item Write \textbf{\fa{سه}} and \textbf{\fa{نه}}, the two whose letters the script chapter gave you.
  \item Say the English cousin of each of the ten. Every one has one.
\end{enumerate}

Then group them by what happened to the first sound: \textbf{haft} shows the \emph{s}-to-\emph{h} rule, \textbf{hasht} borrowed its \emph{h} from \textbf{haft}, and \textbf{shesh} kept its \emph{s} because the rule only touches the front of a word.

Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
